abstract: This lecture reviews the basics of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), a common age-related condition causing lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS). The speaker emphasizes that BPH is a symptom-based diagnosis supported by history, digital rectal exam, and selective laboratory tests. Management includes lifestyle modifications, alpha blockers, 5-alpha reductase inhibitors, and surgical options like TURP. The lecture distinguishes between obstructive and irritative symptoms and highlights the utility of the IPSS score for quantification.
key_points: BPH is benign hyperplasia (increased cell number, not cell size) causing lower urinary tract symptoms; prevalence is 50% at age 50 and 80% at age 80.
Diagnosis requires symptoms; it is not a radiologic or physical exam diagnosis alone.
Lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) are classified as obstructive (weak stream, hesitancy, straining, incomplete emptying, post-void dribbling) or irritative (frequency, urgency, nocturia, dysuria).
The IPSS (International Prostate Symptom Score) is a validated tool to quantify symptoms and should be used, especially when objective measurement is needed.
Digital rectal exam is mandatory in symptomatic patients to assess prostate size (big vs. not big) and to check for nodules.
Urinalysis should be performed to rule out hematuria, infection, or other pathology.
PSA can be supportive but is not diagnostic for BPH; a very low PSA (<0.1) may indicate hypogonadism warranting testosterone evaluation.
Percent-free PSA can help in gray zones: low percent-free suggests higher malignancy risk, high percent-free is more associated with BPH.
First-line management includes lifestyle changes: avoid fluids after 6 PM, limit caffeine, alcohol, and carbonated drinks; double voiding before bed.
Medical therapy includes alpha-blockers (relax prostate/bladder neck) and 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (reduce prostate volume); TURP remains the standard surgical option.
Lifestyle interventions include double voiding, urethral milking, sitting to urinate, and treating constipation to reduce pelvic pressure on the prostate.
Alpha-1 antagonists are first-line for BPH; they relax the prostatic urethra and bladder neck smooth muscle by blocking alpha-1 receptors.
